articles.title: How are you dealing with all the negative side effects of AI on the web?
articles.description:
It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it.

Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result.

I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that.

Edit: I see that most of the replies here are suggesting relying less on the web and going after more fundamental resources, which are great suggestions, don’t get me wrong! But a book from 5 years ago will not help you understand why your custom firmware doesn’t boot in your 1-year old mobile chipset. A existing bug report on the web probably will. Not quite my predicament at the moment, but something very similar for which the web seemed to work just fine before the AI craze.

articles.title: Who wants to crowdsource LLM scans of articles submitted to Lobste.rs?
articles.description:
Like many of us who value the human side of the web, I am looking for ways to keep slop at bay. It seems like LLM detection technology works reasonably well nowadays, with Pangram as the main provider. It is expensive, though!

Assuming pangram scans are trustworthy, and it seems they are, we could create a centralized index of pangram scans of articles. I have already set up a prototype where I publish results of my own pangram scans. I could create more users, each tied to its own API key, so others can contribute with scans as well. This is way more resource efficient than everyone running their own scans.

What do you think?

articles.title: What can I realistically do with local AI on a Mac mini M5 Pro (48GB)?
articles.description:
I just got a Mac mini with an M5 Pro (base CPU config) and 48GB of unified memory. I want to run as much AI locally as makes sense, but it's hard to separate what actually works day to day from benchmark hype.

What I'd like to do:

  • Coding: autocomplete and agentic workflows with local models
  • Image generation
  • Anything else genuinely useful: transcription, RAG over my notes, etc.

Questions:

  1. Which models and quantizations fit comfortably in 48GB and are actually usable, not just "it runs"?
  2. Which runtime and tools: MLX, llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, ComfyUI, something else?
  3. What's your setup, and what did you give up on and go back to cloud APIs for?

Real tokens/sec numbers and "this was a waste of time" stories are especially welcome.
